title: How to Structure a Real Estate Joint Venture Agreement (Step-by-Step Guide)

sections.content: Pooling resources with another investor can unlock deals you could never do alone. A $400,000 fix-and-flip might be out of reach solo, but split the capital and labor with a partner and suddenly it becomes very doable. That is exactly why real estate joint ventures are so popular. But a handshake deal or a casual text thread is not enough. Knowing how to structure a real estate joint venture agreement properly is what separates profitable partnerships from expensive legal nightmares.
What Is a Real Estate Joint Venture?

A real estate joint venture (JV) is a formal arrangement where two or more parties combine money, credit, expertise, or labor to execute a specific deal or series of deals. Unlike a general partnership, a JV is typically deal-specific. Once the project wraps up — the house sells, the building refinances, the land develops — the venture ends. Each party retains their own identity and business outside the JV. This keeps things clean and limits liability to that one project.

JVs show up across every corner of real estate. A wholesaler might JV with a cash buyer to split assignment fees on a distressed property in [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga). A flipper in [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx) might partner with a private lender who funds the deal in exchange for 40% of profits. A buy-and-hold investor in [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) might JV with a local property manager who brings operational know-how. The structure changes, but the need for a solid written agreement never does.
Why You Must Have a Written Agreement

Verbal agreements fall apart the moment money gets tight or a deal goes sideways. Courts rarely enforce them in real estate. A written joint venture agreement defines every party's rights, responsibilities, and remedies before emotions run high. It also helps with lenders, title companies, and attorneys who need to see documented ownership and authority before they will proceed with a transaction.
"A partnership without a written agreement is just a friendship waiting to be tested by money." — Common wisdom among experienced real estate investors
The 8 Core Components of a Real Estate Joint Venture Agreement
1. Parties and Entity Structure

Start by clearly naming every party in the JV. Are they participating as individuals or through their LLCs? Most experienced investors insist on using LLCs to limit personal liability. Specify whether the JV will hold title in one partner's entity, a jointly-owned LLC, or as tenants in common. The structure you choose affects taxes, liability, and how easily you can exit the deal, so consult a real estate attorney before deciding.
2. Roles and Responsibilities

Every JV has at least two roles: the active partner who manages the deal and the passive partner who provides capital or credit. Your agreement must spell out exactly who does what. Who finds the property? Who manages the rehab? Who handles the books? Who communicates with the lender? Ambiguity here causes most JV disputes. Get granular. If Partner A is responsible for the renovation budget, say so in writing.
3. Capital Contributions

Outline exactly what each party is contributing — cash amounts, credit lines, labor, or expertise. Assign a dollar value to non-cash contributions if possible. For example, if one partner is contributing project management worth $20,000 in saved labor costs, document that. Specify when contributions are due and what happens if a partner fails to fund their share on time. Include a capital call clause for unexpected costs, which are common in fix-and-flip deals.
4. Profit and Loss Split

This is the section everyone pays closest attention to, and for good reason. Common splits include 50/50, 60/40, or 70/30, but the right split depends on who is taking the most risk. If one partner funds 100% of the purchase and rehab, a 60/40 split in their favor is reasonable. If both partners contribute equally in cash and labor, 50/50 makes sense. Define the split before profit distributions, preferred returns, or any management fees are paid out. Be specific: state the exact percentage, the order of distributions, and how losses are shared.

Pro Tip: Run your numbers before agreeing to any split. Use the free [Deal Calculator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to model different profit scenarios and make sure the deal actually works for both partners after all costs are accounted for.
5. Decision-Making Authority

Who has the final say? Define which decisions require both partners to agree and which can be made unilaterally. Routine decisions — hiring a contractor, ordering materials — can be handled by the managing partner alone. Major decisions — selling the property, taking on additional debt, approving a budget increase over 10% — should require both partners' written approval. Spell out your voting thresholds and what happens in a deadlock.
6. Timeline and Milestones

Every JV should have a projected timeline. For a fix-and-flip, outline the expected close date, rehab completion date, and target listing date. Include milestone checkpoints so both partners can track progress. If the project runs significantly over schedule, define what happens — does the managing partner take a reduced fee? Can the passive partner exit? A clear timeline holds everyone accountable and gives you a baseline to measure against.
7. Exit Strategies and Dispute Resolution

What if a partner wants out early? What if you disagree on the sale price? Your agreement needs to cover multiple exit scenarios. Common clauses include a buy-sell provision (also called a shotgun clause), where one partner names a price and the other partner must either buy or sell at that price. Also include a dispute resolution process — typically mediation before arbitration — to avoid costly litigation. Never leave these scenarios to chance.
8. Default and Liability Provisions

Define what constitutes a default — missed capital contributions, unauthorized spending, breach of fiduciary duty — and outline the remedies. Include personal guarantee terms if a lender requires them. Clarify each partner's liability ceiling, especially if one party's negligence causes damage. Many JV agreements also include indemnification clauses to protect each partner from the other's misconduct.
A Simple Example: Flip Deal JV Breakdown

Imagine Partner A finds a distressed property worth $250,000 ARV, needs $50,000 in repairs, and can be acquired for $140,000. Partner A brings the deal and manages the renovation. Partner B provides $190,000 in capital (purchase plus repairs plus holding costs). They agree to a 50/50 split after Partner B recoups their capital contribution first. Net profit after all costs comes out to $40,000. Partner B gets their $190,000 back, then each partner receives $20,000. That is a clean, documented structure with no surprises.

items: Always use a real estate attorney licensed in your state to draft or review the agreement
Create a separate bank account for each JV to keep finances clean and auditable
Document every capital contribution and expense with receipts and wire confirmations
Run a background check on potential JV partners before committing to a deal
Include a confidentiality clause if proprietary deal-sourcing methods are involved
File the JV entity (if using an LLC) before the property closes, not after

sections.content: Getting Started: Resources to Build Your Knowledge

If you are new to real estate investing, structuring a JV agreement might feel overwhelming. The good news is that the fundamentals are learnable. Start with a solid foundation by reading the [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) to understand how deals are evaluated and structured. If wholesaling is your entry point, the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) covers how to find and assign deals — a skill that makes you an extremely attractive JV partner to capital-heavy investors.

The best JV partners bring something the other person lacks. If you can source deals that others cannot find, your deal-finding ability is your capital. If you have cash but no time, partnering with a skilled operator makes your money work harder. Understanding your strengths before you approach a JV partner will help you negotiate better terms and build lasting relationships in the business.
